---
title: "Quiz: fitting decays with few photons"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Why do we convolve the model with the IRF ("reconvolution") rather than deconvolve the measured histogram and fit the result?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Recall [the inverse filter](../illposed/lec.qmd) (image formation day, recalled on the deconvolution day).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Deconvolving the noisy histogram divides by the IRF's transfer function, which is small at high frequencies: the noise explodes (an ill-posed problem). Convolving the noise-free model with the IRF is harmless, and comparing it with the raw counts keeps their simple Poisson statistics.
:::

---

**Q2.** A bin expects 0.5 counts. What is the probability that it is empty? Why does the classic χ² with weights $1/y_j$ struggle with such bins?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Poisson: $P(0) = e^{-\mu}$. What is $1/y$ for $y = 0$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$e^{-0.5} = 61\,\%$. A weight of $1/0$ is infinite, so empty bins must be patched (weight 1, or dropped); bins with 1 count get the largest weight of all. And a bin that came out low by chance gets a larger weight than one that came out high, so the fit is pulled downwards: the decay looks faster, τ too short.
:::

---

**Q3.** With an ideal instrument, how many photons do you need for a lifetime with ±5 % precision? With an instrument whose F-value is 1.2?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\sigma_\tau/\tau = F/\sqrt N$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$1/\sqrt N = 0.05$ gives $N = 400$. With $F = 1.2$: $(1.2/0.05)^2 = 576$ photons.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why are two lifetimes so much harder to fit than one?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Can two different pairs of lifetimes give almost the same curve?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sums of exponentials are badly conditioned: quite different pairs (with adjusted amplitudes) give curves that differ by less than the noise, so the cost landscape is a long flat valley. The fit needs many more photons (in the demo, thousands instead of about 100 for 10 %), and lifetimes within a factor of about 2 can hardly be separated at all.
:::

---

**Q5.** A pixel holds two species with equal numbers of molecules (α = 0.5 each), τ = 0.5 and 3 ns. Which fraction of the photons comes from the long species? What are the amplitude- and intensity-weighted mean lifetimes?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Photons per molecule are proportional to its lifetime.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$f = 0.5 \cdot 3/(0.5 \cdot 0.5 + 0.5 \cdot 3) = 0.86$. $\bar\tau_a = 0.5 \cdot 0.5 + 0.5 \cdot 3 = 1.75$ ns; $\bar\tau_f = 0.14 \cdot 0.5 + 0.86 \cdot 3 = 2.64$ ns.
:::

---

**Q6.** Global analysis fits the lifetimes once and then each pixel's amplitudes. Why does this work with far fewer photons per pixel than fitting every pixel separately?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which part of the problem is nonlinear and hard, and how many photons go into it?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The nonlinear, badly conditioned part (the lifetimes) is fitted once from the photons of all pixels, millions of them. What remains per pixel is a linear problem with a few unknowns (the amounts of each species): the same as unmixing with time bins as channels, which is well posed even with a few hundred photons.
:::

---

**Q7.** The residuals of a one-exponential fit are positive at early times, negative in the middle and positive in the tail. What does that tell you?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Residuals of a good fit look like noise.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A systematic wave means the model is missing something: here a second, longer (and a shorter) component. One exponential cannot follow a curve that is steep at first and flat later. Try two lifetimes; the residuals should then look like noise, and the reduced χ² drop to about 1.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Arrival times (no IRF, infinite window) 0.4, 1.1, 2.9, 0.7, 3.6, 1.8, 0.2 and 5.3 ns. What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of τ, and the best possible relative standard error?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Set the derivative of $\sum_i(-\log\tau - t_i/\tau)$ to zero; Cramér–Rao gives $\tau^2/N$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\hat\tau$ = the mean = 16/8 = 2.0 ns. The relative standard error is at least $1/\sqrt 8 = 35\,\%$: eight photons say little.
:::
